title:
At the Pan River Yuan Shao fights Gongsun Zan
Across the Yangtze Sun Jian strikes at Liu Biao
paragraphs:
Now [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) was surrounded by [Liu Biao](char-liu-biao), and his three generals [Cheng Pu](char-cheng-pu), [Huang Gai](char-huang-gai) and [Han Dang](char-han-dang) saved him at the hazard of their lives. He had lost more than half his men. He cut a road through and led the rest home to [Jiangdong](loc-jiangdong). From that day Sun Jian and Liu Biao were enemies.
[Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) meanwhile lay with his army in Henei and was short of grain and fodder, and [Han Fu](char-han-fu), Governor of [Ji Province](loc-ji-province), sent men with grain to keep his troops supplied. [Feng Ji](char-feng-ji), one of Yuan Shao's counselors, said to him: "A great man ranges the realm at will. Is he to live on grain that another sends him? Ji Province is rich in money and grain. Why not take it, General?" Yuan Shao said: "I have no good plan for it." Feng Ji said: "Send a man secretly with a letter to [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan), bidding him march on Ji Province, and promise to fall upon it from both sides at once. He will take the field for certain. Han Fu cannot plan for himself and will beg you to take the province in hand. Then do your work from within, and it is yours for the taking."
[Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) was delighted and sent the letter off to [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan) at once. Gongsun Zan read that they were to attack [Ji Province](loc-ji-province) together and share the land between them, and in his joy he took the field that very day. But Yuan Shao sent another man to give [Han Fu](char-han-fu) secret warning of it. Han Fu in his alarm called in his two counselors, Xun Chen and Xin Ping. Xun Chen said: "Gongsun Zan is driving the men of Yan and Dai straight down upon us, and there is no standing against their first rush. He has [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) with [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) and [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) to help him besides, and we cannot hold out. Now [Benchu](char-yuan-shao) is a man of rare wit and courage, with great captains past counting under his hand. Ask him to govern the province along with you, General. He will treat you handsomely, and you will have no more to fear from Gongsun Zan."
[Han Fu](char-han-fu) sent Guan Chun, his Attendant Officer, to invite [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) in. Geng Wu, his Chief Clerk, spoke against it: "Yuan Shao is a lone guest with a beggared army, and he lives upon our breath. He is an infant in the palm of our hand: stop his milk, and he will starve within the day. Why would you put the province into his keeping? This is to bring a tiger in among the sheep." Han Fu said: "I served the Yuan house once, and I have not [Benchu](char-yuan-shao)'s abilities. The men of old sought out the worthier and gave place to him. Why should you gentlemen be jealous?" Geng Wu sighed: "[Ji Province](loc-ji-province) is done for!" And thirty men and more laid down their offices and went. Only Geng Wu and Guan Chun lay in wait outside the walls for Yuan Shao.
Some days later [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) came up with his army. Geng Wu and Guan Chun sprang out with drawn blades to kill him, but [Yan Liang](char-yan-liang), Yuan Shao's general, cut Geng Wu down where he stood, and [Wen Chou](char-wen-chou) hacked Guan Chun to death. Yuan Shao came into [Ji Province](loc-ji-province), made [Han Fu](char-han-fu) General of Might, and parted the business of the province among [Tian Feng](char-tian-feng), [Ju Shou](char-ju-shou), [Xu You](char-xu-you) and [Feng Ji](char-feng-ji), so that Han Fu was stripped of every power he had. Too late for regret, he left his household behind and rode away alone to [Zhang Miao](char-zhang-miao), Grand Administrator of [Chenliu](loc-chenliu).
Now [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan) learned that [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) had taken [Ji Province](loc-ji-province), and sent his younger brother [Gongsun Yue](char-gongsun-yue) to ask for his share of the land. Yuan Shao said: "Ask your brother to come himself. I have a matter to talk over with him." Gongsun Yue took his leave and set out home. He had not gone fifty li when a body of horse broke out from beside the road, crying: "We are the household men of [Imperial Chancellor Dong](char-dong-zhuo)!" and they shot him dead with arrows. His followers fled back to Gongsun Zan with the news. Gongsun Zan was in a fury. "Yuan Shao drew me into taking arms against [Han Fu](char-han-fu), and then walked in and took the province himself! Now he has shot my brother down and laid it on [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s men. How should such a wrong go unavenged!" He called up every man of his own command and marched upon Ji Province.
[Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) heard that his army was on the way and led his own out as well. The two came together on the Pan River, Yuan Shao's on the east of the bridge there and [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan)'s on the west. Gongsun Zan halted his horse upon the bridge and shouted: "Faithless wretch, how dare you sell my name!" Yuan Shao rode up to the bridge in his turn and pointed at him. "[Han Fu](char-han-fu) was not fit for the job, and yielded [Ji Province](loc-ji-province) to me of his own will. What business is that of yours?" Gongsun Zan said: "I took you once for a loyal and upright man and set you up as chief of the alliance. But now you show yourself a wolf at heart and a cur in all you do. What face have you to stand among men!" A great rage took Yuan Shao. "Who will take him for me?"
Before the words were out, [Wen Chou](char-wen-chou) put his horse forward with his spear levelled and came straight up onto the bridge. [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan) met him at the end of it. They had not fought a dozen bouts when Gongsun Zan could stand against him no longer and fled, and Wen Chou came after him hard. Gongsun Zan ran in among his own lines, and Wen Chou rode at a gallop into the middle, driving this way and that. Four stout generals of Gongsun Zan's came out against him together. Wen Chou ran one of them through and had him down from the saddle, and the other three fled. He chased Gongsun Zan through his own lines, and Gongsun Zan made for a valley in the hills. Wen Chou whipped up his horse and shouted after him fiercely: "Down from your horse and yield!" Gongsun Zan had lost his bow and arrows, and his helmet had fallen from his head. His hair streaming loose, he drove his horse round the slope of a hill; the beast stumbled under him and pitched him down the bank. Wen Chou gripped his spear and came on to run him through, when out from the left of the grassy slope wheeled a young general, who came flying up with his spear levelled and made straight for Wen Chou.
[Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan) scrambled up the bank and looked at the young man. He was eight chi tall, with heavy brows and great eyes, a broad face and a full jaw, and a commanding presence. He fought [Wen Chou](char-wen-chou) fifty bouts and sixty with neither of them getting the better of it. Then Gongsun Zan's rescue came up, and Wen Chou wheeled his horse and went off, and the young man did not follow him. Gongsun Zan hurried down the earthen bank and asked his name. The young man bowed from the saddle and answered: "I am a man of Zhending in Changshan. My surname is Zhao, my name Yun, my style Zilong. I was one of [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao)'s people, but seeing that he had no heart to serve his sovereign or to save the people, I left him to take service under you, and by chance I find you here." Gongsun Zan was well pleased, and they went back to camp together and put the armed men in order.
Next day [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan) drew his horse and foot into two bodies, left and right, spread out like a pair of wings. He had above five thousand horses, and the most of them white. In his old wars against the [Qiang](misc-qiang) he had picked out white horses for the van, and was called the General of the White Horse for it. The Qiang would run at the mere sight of a white horse, so he had come to keep a great many. [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) set [Yan Liang](char-yan-liang) and [Wen Chou](char-wen-chou) in his own van with a thousand bowmen and crossbowmen apiece, and these likewise in two bodies, left and right: those on the left to shoot into Gongsun Zan's right wing, those on the right into his left. Then he put [Qu Yi](char-qu-yi) with eight hundred archers and fifteen thousand foot in the middle of the line, and held some tens of thousands of horse and foot behind them in support.
[Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan) had but newly got [Zhao Yun](char-zhao-yun) and did not yet know his heart, so he gave him a separate force and kept him in the rear, and sent his great general Yan Gang to lead the van. He took the center himself and halted his horse upon the bridge, with his standard planted beside him — a great red ring on it, and the word Commander worked in gold thread. They beat the drums from [chen](misc-double-hours) to [si](misc-double-hours), but [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao)'s army did not come on. [Qu Yi](char-qu-yi) had his archers lie down under cover of their shields and wait for the signal shot before loosing. Yan Gang came on with drums and shouting and drove straight at Qu Yi, whose men lay still and never stirred at the sight of him, until he was close upon them. Then a shot went off, and the eight hundred bows and crossbows were loosed together. Yan Gang swung round to get back, but Qu Yi whipped his horse forward, swung his blade, and cut him from the saddle, and Gongsun Zan's army was broken. The two wings would have come to the rescue, but [Yan Liang](char-yan-liang) and [Wen Chou](char-wen-chou) held them off with their bowmen. Yuan Shao's whole line came forward and carried the fight to Jie Bridge, where Qu Yi rode in, cut down the standard-bearer first, and hewed the embroidered banner to the ground.
[Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan) saw the banner go down, turned his horse, and rode off the bridge. [Qu Yi](char-qu-yi) drove his men straight on against the rear, and there came full upon [Zhao Yun](char-zhao-yun), who put his horse at him with the spear levelled and made for him. A few bouts, and a single thrust brought Qu Yi down from his horse. Then Zhao Yun rode alone into [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao)'s army, breaking left and right as though not a man stood in his way. Gongsun Zan brought his men back to the attack, and Yuan Shao's army was routed.
[Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao), for his part, had sent scouts forward, and they came back with word that [Qu Yi](char-qu-yi) had cut down a general, taken a banner, and was after the broken enemy. So he made no preparation, but rode out with [Tian Feng](char-tian-feng) to see it, taking a few hundred halberdiers of his own guard and a few dozen mounted bowmen, and laughing aloud as he went: "A worthless fellow, this [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan)!"
He was still speaking when [Zhao Yun](char-zhao-yun) came charging up before him. The bowmen would have shot, but Zhao Yun ran several of them through one after another, and the rest all fled. Then [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan)'s men ringed them round from behind. [Tian Feng](char-tian-feng) said to [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) in alarm: "Take cover inside that empty wall, my lord!" Yuan Shao dashed his helmet to the ground and cried out: "A man would sooner die fighting in the line! Shall I creep behind a wall and hope to live?" At that the soldiers fought with one heart to the death, and Zhao Yun could not break through them. Then Yuan Shao's main body swept in, with [Yan Liang](char-yan-liang) bringing his force in as well, and the two fell on together. Zhao Yun covered Gongsun Zan and cut a way out through the press, and they came back to Jie Bridge. Yuan Shao drove his army forward and over the bridge after them, and there was no counting those who drowned. He led the chase himself, but he had not gone five li when a great shouting rose behind the hills, and a body of horse burst out with three generals at the head of it — [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei), [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) and [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei). Word had reached them at Pingyuan that Gongsun Zan and Yuan Shao were at war, and they had come to fight for him. Now the three spurred forward together, each with his own weapon, and made straight for Yuan Shao. He was frightened out of his wits. The fine blade fell from his hand to the ground; he wheeled his horse and fled, and his men fought desperately to get him back across the bridge. Gongsun Zan drew off his men as well and went back to camp. When Liu Bei, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei had made their greetings, Gongsun Zan said: "If [Xuande](char-liu-bei) had not ridden so far to save me, I should have come off badly." And he had Zhao Yun brought to meet them, and Liu Bei took such a liking to him that he could not bear to part with him.
[Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao), having lost a battle, held his ground and would not come out, and the two armies lay facing each other for more than a month, until word of it reached [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) at [Chang'an](loc-changan). [Li Ru](char-li-ru) said to him: "Yuan Shao and [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan) are both men of mark in our day, and they are at each other's throats on the Pan River. Borrow the Emperor's name for an edict and send men to make peace between them. Both will be grateful for the favor and will come over to you, Grand Preceptor." Dong Zhuo liked the plan well, and next day he sent Ma Midi the Grand Tutor and Zhao Qi the Minister Coachman off with the edict. The two came into [Hebei](loc-hebei), and Yuan Shao went a hundred li out to meet them and bowed twice as he took it. Next day they went on to Gongsun Zan's camp and proclaimed the edict there. Gongsun Zan sent a man with a letter to Yuan Shao, and the two made peace. Ma Midi and Zhao Qi then returned to the capital with their report. Gongsun Zan marched home that same day, and sent up a memorial recommending [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) for Chancellor of Pingyuan. Liu Bei and [Zhao Yun](char-zhao-yun) parted holding each other's hands, with tears running, neither able to let the other go. Zhao Yun sighed and said: "I was wrong once in taking Gongsun Zan for a hero. Now I see what he does, and he is no better than Yuan Shao and the rest." Liu Bei said: "Bend yourself to his service a while. The day will come when we meet again." And they parted weeping.
[Yuan Shu](char-yuan-shu), meanwhile, was at Nanyang, and hearing that [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) had newly come by [Ji Province](loc-ji-province) he sent to ask him for a thousand horses. Yuan Shao would not give them. Yuan Shu was angry, and from that time the brothers were at odds. He sent also into [Jing Province](loc-jing-province) to borrow two hundred thousand measures of grain from [Liu Biao](char-liu-biao), and Liu Biao would not give it either. Yuan Shu hated him for it, and sent a man secretly with a letter to [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian), urging him to make war on Liu Biao. The letter ran, in substance: "It was my brother [Benchu](char-yuan-shao)'s doing that Liu Biao barred your road before this. Now Benchu is in private treaty with Liu Biao again, and they mean to fall upon [Jiangdong](loc-jiangdong). Take arms quickly and make war on Liu Biao, and I will take Benchu for you, so that both wrongs are paid. You shall have Jing Province and I Ji Province. Do not fail in it!"
[Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) had the letter, and said: "Curse [Liu Biao](char-liu-biao)! He cut off my road home once, and if I do not take the moment now and pay him for it, when shall I?" He called [Cheng Pu](char-cheng-pu), [Huang Gai](char-huang-gai), [Han Dang](char-han-dang) and the rest into his tent to consider it. Cheng Pu said: "[Yuan Shu](char-yuan-shu) is full of guile and not to be trusted." Sun Jian said: "I mean to have my own revenge. Why would I need Yuan Shu's help?" So he sent Huang Gai down to the river first to get the warships ready, with arms and grain loaded aboard them and the horses in the great ships, and set a day to march. Spies on the river learned of it and brought word to Liu Biao, who was much startled and called his officers, civil and military, together in haste. [Kuai Liang](char-kuai-liang) said: "There is no need to be troubled. Let [Huang Zu](char-huang-zu) lead the men of [Jiangxia](loc-jiangxia) out in the van, while you follow with the men of Jing and Xiang in support, my lord. Sun Jian comes across rivers and over lakes — how can he bring his strength to bear?" Liu Biao thought well of it. He bade Huang Zu make ready, and brought up his great army behind.
Now [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) had four sons by [Lady Wu](char-lady-wu). The eldest was [Sun Ce](char-sun-ce), styled Bofu; the second [Sun Quan](char-sun-quan), styled Zhongmou; the third [Sun Yi](char-sun-yi), styled Shubi; the fourth [Sun Kuang](char-sun-kuang), styled Jizuo. [Lady Wu's younger sister](char-lady-wu-sister) was Sun Jian's second wife, and she bore him a son and a daughter besides: the son [Sun Lang](char-sun-lang), styled Zaoan, and the daughter [Sun Ren](char-sun-ren). Sun Jian had also taken a son of the Yu family into his own house, [Sun Shao](char-sun-shao), styled Gongli. And he had a younger brother, [Sun Jing](char-sun-jing), styled Youtai.
As [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) was setting out, [Sun Jing](char-sun-jing) brought the sons to kneel in a row before his horse, and spoke against it: "[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) has all power in his hands, the Son of Heaven is weak, and all within the seas is in uproar, each lord the master of his own quarter. [Jiangdong](loc-jiangdong) has but now come to a little peace, and to raise a great army over one small grudge is ill done. I beg you to reconsider." Sun Jian said: "Enough of this, brother. I mean to range the realm at will. Am I to leave an injury unpaid?" Then his eldest son [Sun Ce](char-sun-ce) said: "If you must go, father, let me go with you." Sun Jian allowed it, and the two took ship together and drove for [Fancheng](loc-fancheng).
[Huang Zu](char-huang-zu) had bowmen and crossbowmen lying along the bank, and when the ships came in to shore they let fly a storm of arrows. [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) ordered his men not to stir, but to lie close in the ships and draw the enemy on by sailing in and out. For three days the ships came in to shore some scores of times, and Huang Zu's men did nothing but shoot, until their arrows were all spent. Then Sun Jian pulled out of his ships the arrows they had gathered, something over a hundred thousand of them. The wind set fair that day, and he had his soldiers loose, until those on the bank could not hold their ground and fell back.
[Sun Jian](char-sun-jian)'s men came ashore. [Cheng Pu](char-cheng-pu) and [Huang Gai](char-huang-gai) parted their force in two and bore straight down on [Huang Zu](char-huang-zu)'s camp, while [Han Dang](char-han-dang) drove his men hard up behind. Pressed on three sides, Huang Zu was badly beaten. He gave up [Fancheng](loc-fancheng) and fell back into Dengcheng. Sun Jian left Huang Gai to keep the ships and led the pursuit himself. Huang Zu came out to meet him and drew up in the open field, and Sun Jian set his own ranks and rode out before the gate of his line, with [Sun Ce](char-sun-ce) reined up at his father's side in full armor, his spear levelled. Huang Zu brought two generals out with him, Zhang Hu of [Jiangxia](loc-jiangxia) and Chen Sheng of [Xiangyang](loc-xiangyang). Huang Zu raised his whip and railed at them: "Rats and thieves of [Jiangdong](loc-jiangdong)! How dare you break into the borders of the imperial house of Han!" And he sent Zhang Hu out to challenge. Han Dang came out of Sun Jian's line to meet him. The two horses closed, and they had fought thirty bouts and more when Chen Sheng, seeing Zhang Hu's strength fail, came flying up to help him. Sun Ce saw it, steadied the spear in his hand, drew his bow and loosed, and the arrow took Chen Sheng full in the face. He came down from the saddle as the string sounded. Zhang Hu saw Chen Sheng fall, and the shock of it caught him off guard. Han Dang's blade took half his head off. Then Cheng Pu spurred to the front of the line to take Huang Zu, and Huang Zu threw away his helmet, left his horse, and got in among the footmen to save his life. Sun Jian cut down the fugitives as far as [the Han River](loc-han-river), and bade Huang Gai bring the ships up to lie there.
[Huang Zu](char-huang-zu) gathered up what was left of his men and came to [Liu Biao](char-liu-biao), telling him there was no standing against [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian)'s force. Liu Biao in his alarm called in [Kuai Liang](char-kuai-liang) to advise him. Kuai Liang said: "We are freshly beaten and the men have no heart for a fight. We can only keep behind deep ditches and high walls, and let their first attack go by, while we send secretly to [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) for help. The siege will raise itself." [Cai Mao](char-cai-mao) said: "[Zirou](char-kuai-liang)'s counsel is a poor one. The enemy is at the foot of our wall and his generals are on the river. Are we to fold our hands and wait to be killed? I am of no great parts, but give me men to lead out of the city, and I will settle it in one battle." Liu Biao gave him leave.
[Cai Mao](char-cai-mao) led above ten thousand men out of [Xiangyang](loc-xiangyang) and drew up on [Mount Xian](loc-mount-xian). [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) came on in full career with his victorious army. Cai Mao rode out. Sun Jian said: "That is the brother of [Liu Biao](char-liu-biao)'s second wife. Who will take him for me?" [Cheng Pu](char-cheng-pu) levelled his iron-spined spear and went out against him. Within a few bouts Cai Mao broke and ran. Sun Jian pushed his whole army forward, and the dead lay strewn across the field. Cai Mao fled into Xiangyang. [Kuai Liang](char-kuai-liang) said that he had refused good counsel and brought on this great defeat, and that by the law of the army he should lose his head. But Liu Biao had lately married his sister, and did not punish him.
[Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) parted his force to the four sides of [Xiangyang](loc-xiangyang), shut the city in, and attacked it. Then one day a wild wind sprang up and snapped the staff of the commander's banner in the center camp. [Han Dang](char-han-dang) said: "This is no lucky sign. We had best draw off for the present." Sun Jian said: "I have fought and won over and over, and Xiangyang will be mine within a day or two. Am I to break off the war because the wind has broken a flagstaff?" So he would not listen to Han Dang, and pressed the attack harder than before. [Kuai Liang](char-kuai-liang) said to [Liu Biao](char-liu-biao): "I watched the sky last night and saw a general's star about to fall. Reckoning by [field allotment](misc-field-allotment), it must answer to Sun Jian. Send a letter to [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) quickly, my lord, and ask his help."
[Liu Biao](char-liu-biao) wrote the letter and asked who would dare break out through the siege with it. A stout general named [Lü Gong](char-lu-gong) answered at once that he would go. [Kuai Liang](char-kuai-liang) said: "Since you dare go, hear my plan. Take five hundred horse and foot, with as many good bowmen among them as you can, and break out through their lines. Then make for [Mount Xian](loc-mount-xian). They will send men after you for certain. Put a hundred of yours up the hill to gather stones and have them ready, and a hundred with bows and crossbows in ambush in the wood. When the pursuit comes up, do not run straight on, but wind and double and draw them to the place of the ambush; then let stones and arrows go together. If you succeed, send up a string of signal shots, and the city will come out to your aid. If there is no pursuit, give no signal, but ride on your way. The moon is dim tonight, and you may go out of the city at dusk."
[Lü Gong](char-lu-gong) took his orders and got his men ready. At dusk they opened the east gate quietly, and he led them out of the city. [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) was in his tent when he heard the shouting, and he got to horse in haste with thirty-odd riders and came out of camp to see. A soldier reported that a body of cavalry had cut its way out and gone off toward [Mount Xian](loc-mount-xian). Sun Jian did not wait to call his generals, but rode after them with the riders. Lü Gong had already laid his men above and below among the thick trees of the hill. Sun Jian's horse was fast, so he outstripped the rest and came on alone, with the men he chased not far ahead of him. "Stand!" he shouted. Lü Gong reined round and came back to fight him. They closed, and at a single bout Lü Gong broke away and slipped into a path among the hills. Sun Jian went in after but lost sight of him. He was climbing up the hill when a gong sounded, and the stones came pelting down from above while the arrows flew out of the wood together. Sun Jian took the stones and the arrows in his body, his brains ran out, and horse and man died there on Mount Xian. He was but thirty-seven years old.
[Lü Gong](char-lu-gong) cut off the thirty riders and killed every one of them, then sent up the string of signal shots. [Huang Zu](char-huang-zu), [Kuai Yue](char-kuai-yue) and [Cai Mao](char-cai-mao) led their men out of the city by separate ways, and the army of [Jiangdong](loc-jiangdong) fell into confusion. [Huang Gai](char-huang-gai) heard the shouting shake the sky and brought his naval force up to the fight, where he met Huang Zu face to face. In less than two bouts he captured him alive. [Cheng Pu](char-cheng-pu), guarding [Sun Ce](char-sun-ce), was hunting for a way out when he came upon Lü Gong. He drove forward, and within a few bouts his spear had Lü Gong out of the saddle. The two armies fought on till daybreak then each drew off, and [Liu Biao](char-liu-biao)'s men went into the city. When Sun Ce came back to [the Han River](loc-han-river) he learned that his father had been shot dead, and that Liu Biao's soldiers had carried the body into the city. He wept aloud, and the whole army wept with him. "My father's body is there," he said. "How can I return home?" Huang Gai said: "We have Huang Zu alive here. Let a man go into the city and treat for peace, and we will give Huang Zu for my lord's body."
Before he had done speaking, an officer of the army named [Huan Kai](char-huan-kai) came forward. "I am an old acquaintance of [Liu Biao](char-liu-biao)'s. Let me go into the city as envoy." [Sun Ce](char-sun-ce) allowed it, and Huan Kai went in to Liu Biao and laid the whole proposal before him. Liu Biao said: "I have [Wentai](char-sun-jian)'s body here, and have laid it in a coffin. Send [Huang Zu](char-huang-zu) back quickly, and let both sides lay down their arms and make no more inroads on each other." Huan Kai bowed his thanks and was about to go when [Kuai Liang](char-kuai-liang) came forward from the foot of the hall. "It must not be! I have a word to say, and not a man of the [Jiangdong](loc-jiangdong) army shall get home alive. Let Huan Kai be beheaded first, and then hear my plan." Truly:
> Sun Jian pursued his foe, and now lies dead;
> Huan Kai sued peace, and may yet lose his head.
What became of Huan Kai, the next chapter will tell.

versions.name: Chang'an
versions.description:
The old capital of Han, on the south bank of the Wei River far west of [Luoyang](loc-luoyang). [Gaozu](char-emperor-gaozu) made it his capital at the founding of the dynasty. [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) carried the court here from Luoyang and made it the capital again.
[Show on map](map:Chang'an city)

versions.name: the twelve double hours
versions.description:
The day runs in twelve double hours of two hours each, named for the twelve earthly branches.
zi 11pm to 1am
chou 1 to 3am
yin 3 to 5am
mao 5 to 7am
chen 7 to 9am
si 9 to 11am
wu 11am to 1pm
wei 1 to 3pm
shen 3 to 5pm
you 5 to 7pm
xu 7 to 9pm
hai 9 to 11pm

versions.name: field allotment
versions.description: The doctrine that each region of the sky answers to a certain region of the earth, so that an omen seen in one quarter of the heavens is read as a sign for the lands allotted to it.

versions.name: the Qiang
versions.description: Herding tribes of the northwest beyond the Han border.
